trialRelevantInfo: Garcia Meza was tried in absentia. The origins of the trial go back to late 1983, when relatives of the victims and their political groups (especially the PS-1, the MIR and the COB) abandoned efforts to seek redress through the criminal courts, after months of unsuccessful pressure for court investigations. A committee representing the COB, the National University and ASOFAMD was formed, and, with the backing of PS-1 and MIR deputies, in February 1984 it launched a parliamentary accusation against Garcia Meza and his former associates. However, the case was soon swamped by the successive political crises which led to President Siles Zuazo's resignation in 1985, and it was not until February 25, 1986, that a newly elected Congress voted to press charges, issued indictments and transferred the case to the Supreme Court. The proceeding was known as the "trial of responsibilities" (Juicio de Responsabilidades) (HRW 1992). The trial began in April 1986 and ended in April 1993. Various human rights organizations pushed for the prosecution as plaintiffs in this case. Garcia Meza was eventually extradited from Brazil in 1995 and started serving sentence.

charges: war crimes against prisoners of war under Article 144 of the Criminal Code of the FRY
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; torture; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: The Podgorica Basic Court opened an investigation into 6 former VJ and JNA members in 2007 on suspicion of committing crimes against civilians and prisoners of war at the Morinj prisoner-of-war camp in 1991 and 1992. 169 Croatians were captured and detained in the Morinj camp. The former soldiers were indicted in 2008 by the Chief State Prosecutor, and the trial began in 2009 in the Podgorica Superior Court with one defendant being tried in absentia. In May 2010, the Podgorica Superior Court convicted the defendants of war crimes and gave them sentences ranging from 1.5 to 4 years in prison. On December 6, 2010, the Court of Appeals revoked the first instance decision and ordered a retrial. At the retrial in 2013, four of the six officers were convicted of a total of 12 years in prison. On April 23, 2014, the Court of Appeals upheld the conviction and sentences of the four officers.

Pinochet was indicted in January 2001 by Judge Juan Guzman. He was placed under house arrest but subsequently freed on bail. trialRelevantInfo: In June 2001 an NGO acted as legal representative for 11 communities who were victims of these massacres and filed a criminal suit against Montt ("Association for Justice and Reconciliation (AJR), a collective of 23 Maya associations and survivors of the massacres.") 2012- stripped of immunity 2013- found guilty and sentenced to 80 years by a three-judge panel 2013- guilty conviction overturned on procedural grounds, case returned to different court for rehearing 2015- high-risk court ruled him unfit for trial and that verdicts could only be used for corrective measures on behalf of victims, establishing that he cannot be sent to prison 2017- case restarted 2018- Rios Montt died Rios Montt and José Rodríguez Sánchez went on trial before Guatemala’s Supreme Court on March 19, 2013 to face charges of genocide and crimes against humanity. On May 10, 2013, a three-judge panel found Rios Montt guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity and sentenced him to 80 years in prison. On May 20, 2013, the Constitutional Court overturned the Montt conviction on procedural grounds and returned the case to a different panel for rehearing. Ríos Montt was released from military prison and placed under house arrest. On August 25, 2015, a high-risk court confirmed a medical panel’s diagnosis of vascular dementia and ruled that Rios Montt was unfit for public trial but ordered that the trial continue behind closed doors and with a guardian present. It also ruled that any verdict could be used only for the application of corrective measures on behalf of the victims, establishing that Rios Montt cannot be sentenced to prison. On March 16, 2016, retrial proceedings restarted against Rios Montt and Jose Rodriguez Sanchez. Proceedings had been suspended after the First Court of Appeals ruled that Rios Montt and Rodriguez Sanchez should be tried separately. On October 13, 2017, two separate trials in High Risk Tribunal "B" began against Rios Montt and Rodriguez Sanchez in the genocide case. On April 2, 2018, while facing a retrial on the original genocide charges, Rios Montt passed away before a verdict could be reached.

Rodriguez Sanchez was acquitted of the charges. On May 20, 2013, the Constitutional Court overturned the Montt conviction on procedural grounds and returned the case to a different panel for rehearing. Ríos Montt was released from military prison and placed under house arrest. Rodríguez Sánchez, who had been acquitted, was also returned to house arrest. On March 16, 2016, retrial proceedings restarted against Rios Montt and José Rodríguez Sánchez in the case of genocide involving the Maya Ixil community. Proceedings had been suspended after the First Court of Appeals ruled that Rios Montt and Rodriguez Sanchez should be tried separately. On October 13, 2017, two separate trials began against Rios Montt and Rodriguez Sanchez in the genocide case. On September 27, 2018, Rodriguez Sanchez was acquitted by two of three judges for his involvement in the 1982-83 massacres against the indigenous Ixil population. The justices unanimously held that the abuses were committed by the military, but disagreed on whether it was proven that Rodriguez gave the commands. In 2019, the case against him continued, as the prosecution appealed the September 2018 ruling.

chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: On March 2, 1993, a military court found 11 police officers and 4 soldiers guilty of excessive use of force and handed down prison sentences of seven and a half years to each defendant. The court accepted the defendants' claim of having killed the victims in self-defense during an armed confrontation; it nonetheless refused to exonerate them completely because of their excessive use of force. The court ruling was deemed questionable, as the military courts were heavily biased and gave the defendants much more leniency than expected. In August 1994, an ad hoc military court acquitted 16 military and police officers for the massacre, thus overturning the 1993 decision. Human rights monitors, representatives of the victims, and the two survivors expressed extreme dissatisfaction with the verdict, asserting that the military court had disregarded crucial evidence and testimony demonstrating that the event was a planned massacre. Despite the acquittal, only nine of the defendants in the case were released, while the others remained in prison on charges of similar killings in other areas. Three other defendants did not stand trial, as they had gone into hiding and were fugitives from the law. As of 2022, there was no indication that further prosecutorial activity has been taken against any of the alleged perpetrators, and impunity for the massacre remains.

trialRelevantInfo: Ag Boula's arrest and detention were widely considered either politically or personally motivated and prompted mass Tuareg insurgency in 2005. In order to quell this insurgency, the Nigeran government granted the provisional release of Ag Boula into exile through a Libyan-mediated negotiation. In 2007, a new Tuareg insurgency began with different origins but similar demands. Ag Boula attempted to mediate on behalf of the Tuareg rebels from exile, but faced opposition from the Nigeran government, prompting him to announce that he was joining the rebellion. This move was condemned by the Nigeran government, who claimed that the provisions of his 2005 release were violated and sentenced him to death in absentia on July 13, 2008. Following the February 2010 military junta, Ag Boula returned to Niamey to pressure the junta to incorporate the Tuareg rebels. He was re-arrested for the same crime of murder of Adam Amenge, but released to return to exile on July 5, 2010, and finally acquitted on December 4, 2010, by the Naimey Court of Appeals.

Revelations that some judicial authorities had taken part in the March 2001 protest prompted charges that investigating magistrates were politically motivated. Justice Minister Castelli wrote to the autonomous judiciary's self-governing body (see Section 1.e.) to suggest that prosecutors' plans to attend a May 10 seminar on dissent and globalization, concurrent with their ongoing investigations of the March 2001 protests, were "inopportune." On May 11, a Naples review court ordered the arrested officers freed; however, they remained under investigation at year's end.

trialRelevantInfo: Early in 1992, the Federal Assembly commission charged with screening high of- ficeholders of the Federal Government and other key institutions for past collaboration with the pre-1989 secret police completed its work A commission attached to the Czech Parliament performed the same function for officials at the republic level. The law barred many former Communist party officials, members of the People's Militia, and secret police collaborators from holding a wide range of elective, nomi- native, and appointive government offices, including appointive positions in state-owned companies, academe, and the media, for a period of 5 years. Hundreds of persons were tired, including at least 12 journalists. The screening process was criticized because it was based on the records of the Communist secret police which many thought were incomplete, unreliable, or both. The version of the screening law that applied to most officials provided no mecha- nism for appeal, although the FBIS had a committee that reviewed cases of collabo- rators to assess whether they were witting or unwitting. If an accused collaborator was found to have been unwitting, this could contribute to his exoneration and ulti- mately to keeping his position. The screening process was also criticized as a viola- tion of human rights principles prohibiting discrimination in employment and con- demning collective guilt. Supporters of the screening process cited the political need to prevent those directly responsible for abuses of power and repression during the years of Communist rule from holding high public office during a 5-year transition period to a free society. After the Federal Constitutional Court ruled on November 26 that one provision of the law was illegal, Federal authorities abolished screening under this provision. Although the 1991 law establishing the screening process was a Federal requirement binding on both Republics, it was, at best, carried out in a desultory and incomplete fashion in the Slovak Republic. In September 1992, the Slovak Interior Minister announced that Slovakia, when independent, would repeal the Federal screening law.

His employment at the Radio Television Libre des Milles Collines ("RTLM") was facilitated by President Habyarimana who used his influence with Ferdinand Nahimana, the Director of RTLM, the government radio station. trialRelevantInfo: On 8.6.2000 ex official Jorge Olivera is arrested in Fiumicino, as a request of the French judiciary. Olivera is arrested because he is suspected of disappearing, torturing and killing of Maria Ana Erize Tisseau, a French citizen kidnapped in San Juan (Argentina) in 1976. 8.8.2000 The arrest is upheld by the president of the appellate Court of Rome (Corte di Appello di Roma). 8.11.2000 The Minister of Justice of Italy asked to maintain the detention of Olivera. 8.31.200 The French authorities requested the extradition of the accused to the attorney general of the Appellate Court of Rome. On 9.19.2000 the IV Appellate Court of Rome denies France the request of extradition and allows the liberation of the prisoner. The only retained him guilty of the illegal arrest of Maria Ana Erize Tisseau. They based the decision on the documentation provided by the defense. 9.20.2000. The general prosecutor of the Appellate Court of Rome (Il procuratore generale della Corte d'appello di Roma) presented an appeal to the Supreme Court (ricorso in Cassazione ) against the decision of releasing Jorge Olivera. The General prosecutor challenged the aforementioned order, noting, among many other things, that the court had given "decisive probative value to completely informal documents produced by the defense" 9.21.2000 The Minister of Justice of Italy requests the Italian embassy at Buenos Aires and to Interpol to investigate the documents presented by the defense. The Italian embassy at Buenos Aires transmits a note from the Ministry of External Affairs of Argentina where the anomalies of the evidence presented by the defense are described. All these information is then transmitted from the Ministry of Justice of Italy to the Prosecution. The Superior Council of Justice of Italy (Il Consiglio Superiore della Magistratura) conducted investigations to see whether the decision of the Appellate Court was just. 2.21.2001. Over the basis of the conclusions of the investigation, the invalidity of the evidence was publicly recognized and disciplinary actions against the judges (that accepted false documentation as valid evidence) were ordered.

Johnny Paul Koroma was the leader of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) and a senior leader within the alliance of the AFRC and the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) in Sierra Leone. On 27 May 1997, the AFRC, founded by members of the armed forces of Sierra Leone, seized power in a coup d'tat. The RUF rebels were reportedly invited to join a government of national unity (Junta). At the time the AFRC/RUF coalition was in power its armed forces, in agreement with or under the orders of Koroma, conducted armed attacks against the civilian population throughout the territory of Sierra Leone. Humanitarian aid workers as well as the UN peacekeeping forces were also targeted. The primary aim of these violent attacks was to terrorize the population and to punish it for not lending sufficient support to the RUF/AFRC alliance. On 7 March 2003, Koroma was indicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone. He was charged with crimes against humanity and war crimes on the basis of individual criminal responsibility. He was also held responsible as hierarchical superior for criminal acts committed by his subordinates. Johnny Paul Koroma went into hiding and was never arrested. On 1 June 2003 Koroma was officially declared dead in neighbouring Liberia under contentious circumstances, although the indictment against him remains in force.

Also, Vice Chairman and member of the Junta governing body (in 1997 AFRC/RUF joined forces and became known as the junta). The AFRC/RUF controlled the government from May 1997 to February 1998. Sankoh was incarcerated in Nigeria and Sierra Leone from March 1997 to April 1999 but still remained the active leader of the RUF and senior leader within RUF/AFRC alliance. Foday Saybana Sankoh was the founder and top commander of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and one of the major leaders of the alliance between the RUF and the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC). The RUF was formed in 1988/1989 and entered Sierra Leone in 1991 to launch a 10-year terror campaign within its territory. The violent strikes were directed against the civilian population, humanitarian assistance operations and UN peacekeepers and resulted in mass murders and pillaging. Sankoh's forces used brutal tactics to seize and maintain control over Sierra Leone's diamond mines, including extensive use of child soldiers and sexual enslavement as a means of terrorising civilians into submission. In 1971, Sankoh was dismissed from the Sierra Leone army and imprisoned for his part in an attempted coup against the president. In 1998, Sankoh had been condemned to death for treason by the High Court of Justice in Freetown, but pardoned the following year after the RUF signed the Lom Peace Agreement with the government granting the rebels a blanket amnesty for their atrocities. He was re-arrested in 2000. Foday Saybana Sankoh and three other leaders of the RUF were indicted separately on 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity by the Special Court of Sierra Leone in March 2003. position_desc: alleged to have been a senior officer and commander of the Revolutionary United Front of Sierra Leone, and between 1998 and 2002, to have been Overall Security Commander in the RUF/AFRC forces
position_desc_fr: aurait été un officier supérieur et un commandant du Front révolutionnaire uni de Sierra Leone et, entre 1998 et 2002, aurait été commandant général de la sécurité au sein des forces du RUF/AFRC
accusedNotes: Augustine Gbao, aka Augustine Bao, is alleged to have been a senior officer and commander of the Revolutionary United Front of Sierra Leone. From March 1999 until January 2002, he was also the joint Commander of the RUF/AFRC forces in the Makeni area. He was first taken into custody on 10 March under Rule 40 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which allows for a suspect to be detained for up to 30 days before being indicted. He was transferred to the Court's custody on 20 March. Gbao was subsequently indicted by the Prosecutor on 16 April 2003, and the indictment was approved the same day by Judge Bankole Thompson. He was charged with 17 counts of crimes against humanity, Violation of Article 3 Common to the Geneva Conventions and of Additional Protocol II (commonly known as war crimes), and other serious violations of international humanitarian law. (An 18th count was later added.) Gbao made his initial appearance on 25 April, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges. Augustine Gbao, also known as Augustine Bao, a former police officer, was born on 13 August 1948 in Blama in the district of Kenema, Sierra Leone. According to the bill of indictment, at the time of the alleged events, Gbao was a senior officer and Commander in the RUF (Revolutionary United Front) in the Junta as well as in the RFU/AFRC (Armed Forces Revolutionary Council). He reportedly joined the RUF in 1991 in Liberia. Before the coup, he was alleged to have been Commander of the RUF Internal Defence Unit and between 1996 and 1998 Senior Commander of the RUF in control of the region of Kailahun. During this period he was said to be subordinate only to the RUF Battlefield Commander, as well as to Foday Sankoh and Paul Koroma, respectively the leaders of the RUF and the AFRC. Between 1998 and 2002, he was alleged to be Overall Security Commander in the RUF/AFRC forces, a position in which he was said to have been responsible for all of the Intelligence and Security units within the RUF/AFRC forces, and subordinate only to Foday Sankoh and Paul Koroma. From March 1999 until January 2002, he was also the joint Commander of the RUF/AFRC forces in the Makeni area. According to the accusation, Augustine Gbao, personally or in concert with other leaders of the RUF and the AFRC, exercised control, authority and command over subordinates in the RUF, the Junta and the armed forces of the RUF/AFRC. During the period covered by the indictment, the RUF and the AFRC, acting in concert with, or under the orders of Gbao led a campaign of armed attacks throughout the territory of Sierra Leone, according to the bill of indictment. The principal targets of these attacks were civilians and humanitarian assistance personnel as well as United Nations peacekeepers. These attacks were carried out primarily to terrorize the civilian population, but were also used to punish the population for failing to provide sufficient support to the RUF/AFRC alliance.

accusedNotes: Alex Tamba Brima was a senior member of the AFRC, Junta and the AFRC/RUF forces in Sierra Leone. He belonged to a group of the AFRC soldiers which staged the coup and ousted the democratically elected government of President Kabbah in May 1997. Brima was a member of the Junta governing body. Brima worked in concert with Charles Taylor. Shortly after this Coup, the AFRC formed an alliance with a rebel movement RUF (Revolutionary United Front). At the time the AFRC/RUF coalition was in power its armed forces organised attacks against the civilian population. The attacks were notable for summary executions, mutilations, pillaging, abductions, and rapes, forced labour and by the enlistment and use of child soldiers. The aim of these attacks was to terrorise the civilian population and to punish it for support given to the regime of President Kabbah. The UN peacekeeping forces were also targeted. During this time, Alex Tamba Brima was considered to have held a leadership position within the AFRC/RUF alliance. Alex Tamba Brima was indicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone on 7 March 2003. He was charged with 18 counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes. Alex Tamba Brima was arrested and transferred to the SCSL on 10 March 2003. At his initial court appearances on 15 and 17 March 2003, he pleaded not guilty to all of the charges. On 20 June 2007, Alex Tamba Brima and his co-defendants were found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity by the SCSL. On 19 July he was sentenced to 50 years' imprisonment. This sentence was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber on 22 February 2008.

name: Ibrahim Bazzy Kamara AKA Brima
position_desc: a senior member of Revolutionary United Front (RUF), the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) and the Junta
position_desc_fr: un membre important du Front révolutionnaire uni (RUF), du Conseil révolutionnaire des forces armées (AFRC) et de la junte
accusedNotes: Brima Bazzy Kamara was alleged to have been a member of a group of 17 soldiers which took power by force on 25 May 1997 in Freetown and overthrew the democratically elected government of President Ahmed Tejan Kabbah. Kamara was a member of the Junta governing body. Kamara worked in concert with Charles Taylor. Shortly after this Coup, the rebel movement RUF (Revolutionary United Front) which had been waging war against the government since 1991, was invited by Johnny Paul Koroma to abandon its rebel movement and share power. This proposition was accepted by Foday Sankoh, the leader of the rebels who, at the time, was under house arrest in Nigeria. Brima Bazzy Kamara allegedly participated in the government thus set up and was nominated by Johnny Paul Koroma to the post of Public Liaison Officer as well as to being a member of the AFRC Supreme Council, both of which posts he held until the arrival of the West African Intervention Force (ECOMOG) which, in 1998, reinstated the democratically elected government of President Ahmed Tejan Kabbah. The AFRC/RUF forces at this point retreated to the centre of the country. At the time the AFRC/RUF coalition was in power, its armed forces were accused of attacking the civilian population, and of committing crimes against humanity and war crimes in the district of Bo in June 1997 and, between May 1997 and February 1998, in the district of Kenema. The aim of these attacks was to wreak terror on the civilian population and to punish it for the purported passive support given to the regime of President Kabbah. Between the month of February 1998 and 30 April 1998, Brima Bazzy Kamara was a Commander of the AFRC/RUF forces in the district of Kono in the east of Sierra Leone. In addition he was suspected of having been one of the Commanders of the AFRC/RUF forces which conducted armed operations throughout the north, the east and the centre of the country. These operations, amongst other outcomes, led to attacks against the civilian population in the departments of Kailahun, Kono, Koinagugu and Bombali between mid-February 1998 and 31 December 1998. Once again, the aim of these attacks was to wreak terror on the civilian population and to punish it for the purported passive support given to the regime of President Kabbah. On 6 January 1999, Freetown was once again overrun and occupied for three weeks by the AFRC/RUF forces. Brima Bazzy Kamara was alleged to have been one of the Commanders who led the attack against Freetown and who directed ground operations. These operations were marked by the great number of atrocities committed against the civilian population of Freetown as well as against the civilian population living in the region surrounding the capital. The aim of these attacks was to punish the population of Freetown and its surroundings for their supposed passive support given to the regime of President Kabbah. The same troops were also alleged to have committed atrocities in the district of Port-Loko from February to April 1999. During all of this time, Brima Bazzy Kamara was always considered to have held a leadership position within the AFRC/RUF alliance. All of these attacks against the civilian populations between May 1997 and April 1999 were notable for their summary executions, mutilations, looting and burning of villages, violations of sexual integrity, forced marriages, abductions and forced labour, particularly in the diamond mines, and by the enlistment and use of child soldiers. Finally, the AFRC/RUF troops were accused of attacking the United Nations peacekeeping forces between the months of April and September 2000. Brima Bazzy Kamara was arrested and transferred to the SCSL (Special Court for Sierra Leone) on 29 May 2003.

accusedNotes: Santigie Borbor Kanu was a senior member of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), the Junta and the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) anti-government forces involved in the Sierra Leone civil war. Kanu was a member of the group who staged the coup that ousted the government of President Kabbah. Brima was an appointed public liaison officer within the AFRC. Brima was a member of the Junta governing body. Kanu worked in concert with Charles Taylor. In May 1997, a group of AFRC soldiers, including Santigie Borbor Kanu, organised and conducted the Coup in Freetown. After the successful overthrow of the government of President Kabbah, the rebel RUF movement made an alliance with the AFRC. At the time the AFRC/RUF coalition was in power in 1997-1999, its armed forces launched a series of attacks against the civilian population. The violent campaign consisted of summary executions, mutilations, destruction of villages, rapes, forced labour and the use of child soldiers. The aim of this violence was to terrorise the civilian population and to deter it from giving support to the regime of President Kabbah. Santigie Borbor Kanu was indicted on 15 September 2003 with 18 counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes. He was arrested the following day. In the beginning of 2004, the SCSL ordered the joint trial of Alex Tamba Brima, Santigie Borbor Kanu and Brima Bazzy Kamara. On 20 June 2007, the three co-defendants were found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity by the SCSL. Santigie Borbor Kanu was sentenced to 50 years imprisonment. This sentence was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber on 22 February 2008. The judgments in the AFRC case were the first delivered by the Special Court. It was also the first time that an international tribunal ruled on the charge of child soldiers conscription, and on the crime of forced marriage in an armed conflict.

accusedNotes: Moinina Fofana was one of the top leaders of the Civil Defence Forces (CDF) in Sierra Leone. The CDF was a pro-government paramilitary organisation involved in an armed conflict against the combined forces of the Revolutionary United Front and the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (RUF/AFRC) during the civil war from 1991-2002. As National Director of War of the CDF, Fofana was considered the second in command after Samuel Hinga Norman. He was in charge of liaising with the commanders in the field and of supervising and controlling operations; he provided them with logistics including arms and ammunition. From 1996 to 1999, the CDF forces actively fought against the RUF/AFRC in various parts of the country. The attacks were also directed against civilians suspected of collaborating with the rebels and included killings, looting, and the destruction of private property. Moinina Fofana was arrested on 29 May 2003 and transferred to the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL). In the indictment against him of 26 June 2003 he was charged on the basis of individual responsibility with crimes against humanity and war crimes. In addition, the indictment held him and other leaders of the CDF to be responsible as hierarchical superiors for acts committed by their subordinates. On 2 August 2007 the Court convicted Moinina Fofana on four counts involving violence to life, in particular murder, cruel treatment, pillage and issuing collective punishments. On 9 October 2007, Fofana was sentenced to 6 years imprisonment. In its Appeals Judgement of 28 May 2008, the Appeals Chamber entered new convictions against Fofana for murder and inhumane acts as crimes against humanity and increased his sentence to 15 years' imprisonment.

trialRelevantInfo: On September 22, 2007, Chile extradited Fujimori to face an array of charges relating to corruption and human rights violations during his presidency. On December 11, 2007, Peru's Supreme Court convicted Fujimori and sentenced him to six years in prison for ordering an illegal search. At year’s end, Fujimori remained in jail pending trial for the additional corruption and human rights charges. On April 7, 2009, the Supreme Court’s three-judge Permanent Criminal Chamber convicted Fujimori of human rights violations in the 1991 Barrios Altos and 1992 La Cantuta killings, for which he was sentenced to 25 years in prison. The charges in that conviction included murder, aggravated kidnapping and battery, and crimes against humanity. The corruption and human rights sentences were to be served concurrently. On July 20, 2009, the Supreme Court convicted Fujimori on bribery charges and sentenced him to 7.5 years in prison. He was accused of giving a $15 million bribe to his former spy chief, Vladimiro Montesinos. On September 30, 2009, once again facing a criminal trial before the Supreme Court, Fujimori pled guilty to charges of illegal wiretapping and embezzlement, for which he received another 6-year sentence. On December 30, 2009, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Fujimori on the corruption and human rights charges. On August 11, 2011, the Constitutional Tribunal rejected Fujimori’s habeas corpus petition, once again confirming his 2009 sentence of 25 years’ imprisonment for authorizing the mass killings at Barrios Altos and La Cantuta. Fujimori was granted a pardon by a judge in 2017, but in 2019, the pardon was annulled and he was sent back to prison.

chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted; other
trialRelevantInfo: Viktor Lozynskiy, Mykhailo Kovalsky, and Yevhen Horbenko were all linked to the death of Valeriy Oliynyk that occurred on June 16, 2009. The three pursued Oliynyk into a wooded area where they assaulted him, broke his leg, and shot him multiple times. In April 2011, Yevhen Horbenko was sentenced to 9 years in prison, while Mykhailo Kovalsky received a 5-year suspended sentence, and Viktor Lozinsky was sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. Lozinsky’s sentence was reduced at appeal level to 14 years in March 2012. In March 2013 the High Specialized Court on Civil and Criminal Cases reduced Lozinsky’s sentence from 14 to 10 years imprisonment, apparently finding some extenuating circumstances. In February 2016, Lozinsky received early release, but it was announced in March that the prosecutor had appealed against the early release, and the then Prosecutor General Yuri Lutsenko even asserted in April 2017 that the High Specialist Court had overturned the early release. It is not at all clear what happened to that ruling, which should have been final, since Losinsky appears to have been at liberty since 2016.

charges: War crimes against civilians, killing 118 Albanians
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; murder or killing, incl attempted; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Former members of the 177th Yugoslav Army Intervention Squad known as the “Jackals,” were arrested in 2010 and indicted by the Serbian war crimes prosecutor (Bruno Vekaric) on suspicion of having committed war crimes in Kosovo in 1999 during the armed conflict. The charges alleged that Milojko Nikolic, Dejan Bulatovic, Ranko Momic, and Radoslav Brnovic killed 118 Albanians and set fire to over 40 houses. Nikolic was extradited to Serbia to face charges in 2010. On February 11, 2014, nine defendants were convicted of war crimes against civilians in the Belgrade Special Court and sentenced to a total of 106 years in prison. The Court of Appeals in Belgrade overturned the verdict on February 26, 2015 and sent the case back for retrial, which began that same year. Momic escaped detention and fled to Ukraine in 2015, and trial proceedings against him were separated. Trial proceedings against Brnovic were terminated when he died on September 29, 2015. Trial proceedings against Bulatovic were dismissed on January 25, 2016 as he became too ill to face trial. Nikolic died on July 5, 2017 before the retrial verdict was issued, and trial proceedings were terminated against him. In July 2019, the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor issued a joint indictment combining the current case with an indictment against Predrag Vukovic, another former member of the unit, for the same crimes. The trial was postponed at least five times due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the verdict appears to be pending still.

trialRelevantInfo: The complaint against the accused was accepted in March 2000 by Judge Guillermo Ruiz Polanco who, on top of acknowledging the international character of the alleged crimes, justified the appropriateness of the Spanish jurisdiction on the lack of territorial proceedings. In June 2006, Investigative Judge Santiago Pedraz issued arrest warrants for 8 individuals implicated in this case, including Rios Montt. The Guatemalan Supreme Court acted on the Spanish judicial request by ordering the arrest of all persons named in the Spanish warrant, except Rios Montt. Subsequent court decisions excluded former heads of state Efrain Rios Montt and Oscar Humberto Mejia Victores from the warrant. On December 12, 2007, the Constitutional Court ruled that Spain did not have jurisdiction over crimes committed in Guatemala and denied the extradition of Efrain Rios Montt and the other accused. The accused were never extradited to Spain, and no trial resulted from the Spanish indictment. Rios Montt stood trial for a separate set of genocide charges in Guatemala in 2013 and was found guilty of genocide, but the Guatemalan Constitutional Court overturned the conviction.

trialRelevantInfo: On September 17, 2012, authorities indicted Ferney Tapasco for ordering the killing of Orlando Sierra. He was charged with aggravated homicide. Three others were tried alongside Tapasco, but there is no indication that they were state agents, rebels, or paramilitary members. chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted; other
trialRelevantInfo: On March 19, 2010, the Public Ministry charged Italo Del Valle Alliegro with premeditated homicide and violating treaties and international conventions in connection with El Caracazo. On June 28, 2010, the Ninth Court of Appeals in Caracas dismissed the charges, asserting that the period for filing charges had lapsed. On July 2, the Public Ministry asked the Supreme Court to reopen the case. The Supreme Court dismissed various judges involved in the case. On July 29, 2010, the Criminal Cassation Chamber of the Supreme Court of Justice declared the appeals court judges' decision to have been an "inexcusable error" and annulled the court's earlier ruling. In October 2011, it was announced that Alliegro would stand trial for the charges alongside José Rafael León Orsoni, Luis Guillermo Fuentes Serra, and Fredy Ventura Maya Cardona. The outcome of the trial could not be found, and it is unclear whether a verdict was reached in the case.

name: Juan Chiroy Sal
charges: extrajudicial killing, later changed to breach of duties
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted; other
trialRelevantInfo: The Public Ministry (MP) accused Colonel Juan Chiroy Sal of being the main person responsible for the massacre, as well as eight soldiers for the six deaths that occurred during the confrontation. They were accused of extrajudicial killing. In February 2015, Judge Patricia Flores sent the nine soldiers to trial and changed the crime of extrajudicial killing to homicide. In the case of Colonel Juan Chiroy, the crime of extrajudicial execution and attempted extrajudicial execution was changed to the crime of breach of duties. On July 14, 2015, in Court "A" of Higher Risk, a hearing was held to present evidence against Chiroy Sal and the other soldiers accused of perpetrating the massacre. The trial was paused in December 2015. In March 2019, Judge Claudette Domínguez of High Risk Court A moved Colonel Chiroy Sal and the other 8 soldiers to house arrest after they had been waiting for several years in preventative detention. The accused are still awaiting trial. They were expected to begin oral arguments on September 3, 2021.

trialRelevantInfo: Police officers Enzo Pontani, Luca Pollastri, Paolo Forlani, and Monica Segatto were sent to trial in January 2007 for manslaughter and on July 6, 2009, a court in Ferrara sentenced the four police officers to three years and six months each. On June 21, 2012, the Supreme Court of Cassation upheld the conviction of the four police officers to three years and six months’ imprisonment for manslaughter. A pardon by the Italian parliament issued in 2006, while prior to the sentencing did intimately reduce their final sentences by 3 years, leaving the accused to only have six months of sentencing time. Ivory Coast was not party to the Rome Statute at the time the conflict erupted in December 2010. According to articles 12 and 13 of the Rome Statute, the country accepted the ICC's jurisdiction on 18 April 2003 by lodging a special declaration. Later on, on 22 February 2012, Judges expanded the temporal scope of the investigation to include crimes between 19 September 2002 and 28 November 2010. On 30 November 2011 he was transferred to the ICC detention center at The Hague, by the Ivorian authorities. The confirmation of charges hearing in the case took place on 19- 28 February 2013. A warrant of arrest against Charles Ble Goude, Minister of Youth under Gbagbo, was issued under seal on 21 December 2011 and unsealed on 30 September 2013. On 17 January 2013, Ble Goude was arrested in Ghana where he was living. He was extradited to Cote d'Ivoire the following day. On 21 January 2013, he was charged with war crimes, murder, theft of public funds but he was transferred to the Netherlands on 21 March 2014. Charges against him were confirmed on 11 December 2014. name: Felix Tum Ramírez
position_desc: former Rabinal civil defense patrol (PAC) member
position_desc_fr: ancien membre de la patrouille de défense civile (PAC) de Rabinal
charges: sexual violence and crimes against humanity
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; maltreatment and excessive use of force; crimes against humanity
trialRelevantInfo: In May 2018, authorities arrested seven former members of the civil defense patrols, including Ramirez, and charged them with sexual violence against 36 Maya Achi women in Rabinal, between 1981 and 1985. On June 21, 2019, Judge Claudette Dominguez of High Risk Court A ruled there was insufficient evidence to send the former PAC members to trial, and she ordered them released. Judge Dominguez stated that the evidence demonstrated that three of the defendants, Felix Tum Ramírez, Pedro Sánches Cortez, and Simeon Enriquez Gomez, were members of the civil defense patrol, but that the time period in which the documents presented show this are from a different time period that when the alleged crimes were committed. The prosecution filed recusal motions against Judge Dominguez, and in September 2019, the First High Risk Appellate Court granted the recusal motion and transferred the case to Judge Miguel Angel Galvez of High Risk Court B; however, the case remained mired in a series of unresolved appeals. While several other defendants accused in the case would go on to stand trial in 2022, Ramirez was not one of them. Some victims have petitioned the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court to nullify the ruling dismissing the charges against Pedro Sánchez Cortez, Simeon Enríquez Gomez, and Felix Tum Ramírez, but it has yet to happen.

Kyagulanyi (Bobi Wine) has since been arrested, detained, and charged with various offenses several times since becoming a legitimate threat to the current president, Museveni, who has held office since 1986. Pallab was buried by the side of Kalapani Jheel along with several other bodies. Pallab was taken to an Eidgah at Mirpur-12, where he was shot to death. Charge 2: On 27 March 1971, Quader Molla's aides murdered pro-liberation poet Meherun Nesa, her mother and two brothers at their house at Mirpur-6. Charge 3: On 29 March 1971, Abdul Quader Molla along with other members of Al Badr, Razakar and non-Bangalees detained Khandakar Abu Taleb from Mirpur 10 bus stand and tied him up with a rope. He was brought to the Mirpur Jallad Khana Pump House and killed. Charge 4: On 25 November 1971, Quader Molla with his 70 accomplices went to the village of Khanbari and Ghotan Char, now Shaheed Nagar of Keraniganj, and abducted two unarmed freedom fighters from the house of Mozaffar Ahmed Khan. Freedom fighters Osman Gani and Golam Mostafa were brutally murdered by charging bayonet. Charge 5: Attack and indiscriminate shooting by Quader Molla and his gang killed hundreds of unarmed people of the two villages. Among them, 24 persons were named in the charge. On the early morning of 24 April, members of Pakistan occupation forces and around 50 non-Bangalees in the presence of Quader Molla raided Alubdi village of Mirpur and attacked unarmed villagers, killing 344 people. Charge 6: On 26 March 1971 in the evening, some Bihari and Pakistani soldiers led by Quader Molla killed Hazrat Ali and five members of his family at Mirpur. Entering his house, the soldiers shot dead Hazrat and killed wife Amina and daughters Khadija and Tahmina. That day they also killed his only son, two-year-old Babu, by bashing the baby against the ground.

accusedNotes: In June an inmate of prison LA-155/18 in the Almaty region, Natalya Slekishina, submitted a complaint to the Almaty police department that she had been raped by several prison officers. According to Slekishina, she tried to report the incident back in August 2015, but the application was not accepted for a long time, and the management of the institution where she was, according to Slekishina, tried to hide her pregnancy. She subsequently gave birth to a child on April 25. DNA tests conducted by the Center of Forensic Examination under the Justice Ministry indicated a DNA match for Ruslan Hakimov, one of the four prison officers mentioned in Slekishina’s complaint, as the child’s biological father. Slekishina’s lawyer, Aiman Umarova, a well-known human rights attorney, insisted the three other officers should be charged with rape as well. According to Umarova, the rape was a kind of punishment for Slekishina from the staff of the detention center after she was asked to serve some kind of middleman between prisoners and authorities. According to her, Slekishina refused the staff of the detention center in their request for which she was repeatedly raped. Umarova argued that other officers who were aware of the crime should also be held liable and that charges for torture should be added to the case, since they failed to stop the rape. Slekishina, who faced pressure and threats while under continued incarceration, chose not to press charges in the case further. The other guards were witnesses in her case. On September 30, Hakimov was sentenced to nine years in prison. Subsequently, in the summer of 2019, Khakimov was released on parole for exemplary behavior. However, in October, the court of the East Kazakhstan region decided to return him to prison at the request of the victim

trialRelevantInfo: On January 4, 2009 a Vietnamese man died in police custody in Brno. Three policemen and the man’s neighbor beat the man, a suspected heroin dealer, in his apartment. On August 31, 2010, the Czech Regional Court in Brno sentenced policeman Josef Srnsky to 3.5 years in prison. Katerina Slavickova, a former neighbour of the Vietnamese, who participated in the beating of him, was given 2.5 years behind bars. The other two policemen, who were watching the attack and did not interfere, were given three-year suspended sentences with a five-year probation. They were also banned from working in security forces for five years. On April 6, 2011, Srnsky’s sentence was extended to 10 years by a Czech appeals court. The neighbor’s sentence was extended to 8 years. The other two officers who were charged received suspended sentences for not intervening. On June 8, 2011, the Brno regional court sentenced the two policemen to three years in prison, thus toughening the suspended sentence it imposed on them previously. The Supreme Court then affirmed the ruling for the four on April 3, 2012.

Tajikistan, however, refused to comply.

accusedNotes: On August 29th, 2015, police detained 23-year-old Umar Bobojonov and a group of his friends while they were walking in Vahdat Park. At the police station, Bobojonov’s friends witnessed police beat Bobojonov until he lost consciousness. Bobojonov died in the hospital on September 4 after a weeklong coma. charges: Torture and extrajudicial killing of Romanian citizen József Bara
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; murder or killing, incl attempted; torture
trialRelevantInfo: On April 8, 2013, two police officers, both from Kiskoros, detained Jozsef Bara, a Romanian man, on suspicion of petty theft. They seriously injured him at the Izsak police station, and he died as a result of those injuries. On April 11, the Kecskemet District Court ordered the pretrial detention of the two officers. On October 1, the Bacs-Kiskun County Chief Prosecutor’s Office pressed charges against the two former officers and two other officers for beating the victim to death and other crimes. On December 17, 2014, the Kecskemet Court sentenced a police officer to life imprisonment for the beating death of ethnic-Hungarian Romanian citizen Jozsef Bara, who was in police custody at the Izsak police station in April 2013 on suspicion of petty theft. A second defendant received a 20-year prison term for his part in the incident. Two other defendants received suspended sentences. On June 19, 2015, the Szeged Court of Appeals reduced the sentences of the two police officers convicted in December 2014 by the Kecskemet Tribunal for the beating death of an ethnic-Hungarian Romanian citizen, Jozsef Bara, while in police custody at the Izsak police station in 2013 on suspicion of petty theft. The appellate court reduced one officer’s prison term from life imprisonment to 12 years and the second officer’s sentence from 20 to 10 years.

name: Mihajlo Hrastov
position_desc: former member of the Karlovac Police Special Forces
position_desc_fr: ancien membre des forces spéciales de la police de Karlovac
accusedNotes: In May of 2000, the long-delayed retrial of soldier Mihajlo Hrastov began. The Supreme Court in 1993 ordered the retrial after Hrastov was acquitted in 1992 of the massacre of 13 Serb prisoners in Karlovac in September 1991. At year's end, the trial was adjourned while the prosecution sought witnesses to the massacre. In September 2002 the retrial of Mihajlo Hrastov, a former member of the Karlovac Police Special Forces, for the murder of 13 Yugoslav National Army prisoners of war near Karlovac in 1991, ended at the Karlovac County Court in acquittal. The Court accepted the defendant's claim that he had acted in self-defense. The same court had acquitted Hrastov of the same charge in a politicized trial in 1992. Although the retrial began in 2000, it was restarted twice, first in 2001 and again in 2002 due to excessive delays between hearings. In addition, the retrial did not begin for more than 3 years following the Supreme Court's decision ordering a new trial. The prosecution appealed the courts decision. In September 2004 the second retrial of Mihajlo Hrastov, a former Croatian member of the Karlovac Police Special Forces, for the murder of 13 unarmed Yugoslav National Army prisoners of war near Karlovac in 1991, began at the Karlovac County Court. The Supreme Court overturned two previous acquittals of Hrastov. In June 2006, the retrial of Mihajlo Hrastov resumed in Karlovac after a year-long suspension due to the defendant's mental health. Hrastov, an ethnic Croat and former member of the Karlovac special police, was charged with the murder of 13 unarmed Yugoslav National Army prisoners in 1991. The Supreme Court overturned two previous acquittals. In March 2007, the Karlovac County Court acquitted Mihajlo Hrastov, a former member of the Karlovac special police, for a third time of killing 13 unarmed Yugoslav Army soldiers in 1991. Consistent with the two previous acquittals that the Supreme Court overturned since 1992, the court found that Hrastov killed the soldiers in self defense as part of a legitimate military action. In May state prosecutors lodged an appeal at the Supreme Court In May, 2009, the Supreme Court convicted Hrastov and sentenced him to eight years in jail. The appeal chamber reduced the sentence to seven years in January of 2011. The Croatian Constitutional court rejected the punishment in November of 2011 because the supreme Court had failed to publish the sentence. Another retrial took place and on September 7, 2012 the Supreme Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to four years in prison. In one of the longest running criminal cases in the country’s judicial history (beginning in 1992), Hrastov was previously acquitted three times by the Karlovac County Court. The prosecutor told media that while satisfied with the guilty verdict, she would appeal the case because the four-year sentence was less than the statutory minimum for war crimes. Hrastov was also appealing the verdict. In May 2015, the Supreme Court upheld his conviction. Hrastov was released from prison in December 2016, 14 months before the end of his four year sentence for time served while in detention.

name: Damir Ivanković
position_desc: member of the Prijedor Police Intervention Squad
position_desc_fr: membre de la brigade d'intervention de la police de Prijedor
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; crimes against humanity
trialRelevantInfo: On August 21, 1992, the accused, acting as members of the Prijedor Police Intervention Squad, persecuted Bosniak and Croat civilians, leading to over 200 deaths. On January 12, 2009, the accused were indicted on charges of crimes against humanity. The defendants pleaded not guilty, and a trial began on March 31, 2009. During trial proceedings, Damir Ivanković, Gordan Đurić, and Ljubisa Cetic were separated from the case, and all three accepted plea deals and got sentences under 15 years. Ivanković was arrested on 2008, indicted in 2009. On June 22, 2009, Ivanković agreed to a plea deal with the prosecutor’s officer, pleading guilty to crimes against humanity and agreeing to testify against the other defendants originally accused. His plea was accepted on June 29, 2009, and he was sentenced to 14 years in prison. On December 21, 2010, the War Crimes chamber of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found Zoran Babić, Milorad Škrbić, Dušan Janković and Željko Stojnić guilty of crimes against humanity, and Babić and Škrbić were sentenced to 22 years, Dušan Janković was sentenced to 27 years, and Željko Stojnić was sentenced to 15 years. Milorad Radaković was acquitted on lack of evidence. The defense appealed, and on February 15, 2013, the War Crimes chamber of the Appellate division of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and upheld Zoran Babić’s sentence of 22 years, shortened Željko Stojnić and Dušan Janković’s sentence to 21 years, and upheld Željko Stojnić’s sentence of 15 years.

trialRelevantInfo: Due to the General Amnesty Law passed in 1993, no one was held accountable for the massacre by the Salvadoran justice system for nearly three decades. A criminal investigation into the massacre began in 1990 but was halted upon passage of the amnesty law. However, the law was overturned in July 2016, which means that members of the Atlacatl Battalion can finally be prosecuted in El Salvador. Two months after the law was ruled unconstitutional, criminal court Judge Jorge Guzmán Urquilla accepted a petition by the victims to re-open the case in the Second Court of the First Instance of San Francisco Gotera. In March 2017, Judge Guzmán Urquilla brought charges against 18 high-ranking military officers, including three retired Generals: Juan Rafael Bustillo Toledo, Rafael Flores Lima, and former Defense Minister José Guillermo García. The charges include murder, aggravated rape, and acts of terrorism. On April 23, 2019, a judge issued an order adding three new charges, including a forced disappearance charge, against the 16 remaining defendants. The defendants appealed that order, which was affirmed by the intermediate appellate court.

name: Zoltan Andrusko
charges: Murder of journalist Jan Kuciak and his fiancée Martina Kusnirova
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: On February 26, 2018, investigative journalist Jan Kuciak and his fiancee, Martina Kusnirova, were killed in their home in Veľká Mača. Kuciak regularly reported on allegations of high-level corruption and documented tax fraud schemes. Their deaths caused widespread protests around Slovakia. Prime Minister Fico created a prosecution team of employees of the General Prosecutor’s Office, Special Prosecutor’s Office, the Interior Ministry, and the Slovak Information Service (SIS) intelligence agency On 27 September 2018, Tomáš Szabó (former police officer), Miroslav Marček (former soldier), Zoltán Andruskó (hitman), and Alena Zsuzsová (businesswoman) were charged with the murder and conspiracy to murder other government officials. On October 21, 2019, prominent businessman Marian Kocner was also indicted on charges of ordering Kuciak’s murder. On 30 Dec 2019, the Specialized Criminal Court sentenced Zoltan Andrusko to 15 years in prison after striking a deal with prosecutors. On 6 April 2020, Marček was sentenced to 23 years in prison. The ruling was appealed to the Supreme Court, which increased his sentence to 25 years. On September 3, 2020, Alena Zsuzsova was acquitted of the murder of Kuciak. She was later convicted in a separate murder case and sentenced to 21 years. On June 15, 2021, the Supreme court overturned her acquittal in the Kuciak murder, and criminal proceedings are still ongoing. Also on 3 September 2020, the Specialized Criminal Court acquitted Marian Kocner for the murder of Kuciak. He had already been sentenced to 19 years in prison in a separate corruption case. On 15 June 2019, the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal for the murder of Kuciak, and criminal proceedings are still ongoing. On 3 September 2020, Tomáš Szabó was found guilty of involvement in the murder of Kuciak and Kušnírová and sentenced to 25 years in prison. His sentence was confirmed by the Supreme Court on 15 June 2021.

In October 2018, the Prosecutor's Office ordered the capture of the alleged perpetrator and presented the request for criminal action. In April 2021, the trial took place in the Usulután juvenile court, as the unnamed perpetrator was only 17 years old at the time of the crime. On April 16, the juvenile judge decided to acquit, but the prosecution appealed the ruling. In June 2021, the San Miguel Chamber of Minors annulled the trial, considering that the crime was against humanity, and ordered a retrial. The case was then moved to the jurisdiction of Judge Víctor Meléndez. On July 6, 2021, Meléndez issued a resolution in which he laid out the possibility of settling the crime. While Salvadoran law does not allow conciliation for the crime of kidnapping, Meléndez invoked a clause of the Law of the Minor Offender that was in force until 1994 and allowed for “the reconciliation of all crimes or misdemeanors.” The kidnapper asked the victim for forgiveness in court, and the two reconciled, which concluded the first trial of crimes perpetrated during the armed conflict to be resolved since the amnesty law was overturned.

Girkin was a senior separatist rebel, along with Sergey Dubinsky. Oleg Pulatov and Leonid Kharchenko were their direct subordinates. Girkin was responsible for shooting down Malaysian Airlines flight MH17 on July 17 2014 in the Donbas and murdering 298 passengers, along with other former Russian intelligence officers, Sergey Dubinsky, Oleg Pulatov and Ukrainian national, Leonid Kharchenko. charges: murder of 298 people on MH flight 17
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: The trial for Igor Girkin, Sergey Dubinsky, Oleg Pulatov, and Leonid Kharchenko for murder is pending at this time, awaiting further proceedings throughout the year. Hearings in the trial began at the District Court of The Hague on March 9, 2020, and the four suspects are being tried in abstenia. The four suspects are believed to be in Russia in hiding. A verdict is not to be expected until September 2022 at the earliest, but prosecutors are asking for life in prison for each suspect. This case involves four suspects all responsible for shooting down a Malaysian flight flying from Amsterdam to Malaysia on July 17, 2014. The flight landed in the Donbas region of Ukraine, which was Russian occupied at the time, causing investigations to occur between countries such as Russia, the Netherlands, Australia, and Ukraine over who was responsible for the crash. In 2018 an investigation concluded that the surface-to-air missile system used to shoot down the airliner over Ukraine, killing all 298 persons on board, came from the Russian military. While the crash occurred in Ukraine and is coded in the Ukrainian sourcebook, a treaty between the Netherlands and Ukraine made it possible for the Netherlands to prosecute in the cases of all 298 victims, regardless of their nationality. This treaty was signed on July 7, 2017 and allowed Netherlands to prosecute all suspects in the case because most victims on the flight were of Dutch citizenship. On March 21, 2018, the Dutch government sent legislation to the parliament, allowing the suspects involved to be prosecuted in the Netherlands under Dutch law. On June 19, 2019, The Dutch Public Prosecution Service issued international arrest warrants for Igor Girkin, Sergey Dubinsky and Oleg Pulatov, and Leonid Kharchenko. Girkin and Dubinsky were senior separatist rebels while Pulatov and Kharchenko were their direct subordinates. Prosecutors accuse the four suspects who were separatist rebels fighting Ukrainian government forces in 2014, of forming a team that aimed to bring down Ukrainian planes using a missile system trucked in from a Russian military base.

trialRelevantInfo: On February 19, 2019, Judge Eduardo Jaime Escalante Diaz of the First Civil Chamber of the Salvadoran Supreme Court was charged with the crime of sexual aggression against a 10-year-old girl. Escalante was arrested by police, but because he was a magistrate of the Chamber, he enjoyed constitutional jurisdiction, so the Legislative Assembly had to submit him to a trial to remove his immunity in order to face criminal proceedings. On March 4, the Legislative Assembly voted to remove his immunity from criminal prosecution. On October 31, 2019, the Criminal Chamber dismissed the sexual assault charges and determined that Escalante’s actions did not constitute a felony, but rather a misdemeanor, because the encounter happened quickly and in a crowded place. This reclassification of the crime meant that the Criminal Chamber would no longer have jurisdiction over the case. The attorney general appealed the decision and asked the Criminal Chamber to overturn the ruling, admit all evidence, and send Escalante to trial. The case eventually reached the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of Justice, which, in March 2022, sentenced Judge Escalante Diaz to 10 years in prison for sexual assault of a minor.

name: Desiré Delano Bouterse AKA Desi Bouterse
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: Suriname gained independence from the Netherlands until 1980, so the countries had a close judicial relationship. Following the rise of complaints coming from the families of the victims, on 20 November 2000 the Amsterdam Court of Appeal allowed Dutch prosecutors to investigate the responsibility of former Suriname military leader. In 2001 there was a ruling which announced that the Dutch courts lacked jurisdiction over Bouterse's case and the accused would have to stand trial in Suriname. This is when the case was transferred back to Suriname. In April 2008, a military court ruled that all suspects involved in the 1982 December murders had to stand trial, including Bouterse. In November 2008, the trial of Bouterse began but faced repeated delays. On 4 April 2012, about two months before the verdict in the trial, the National Assembly passed an amendment to extent the 1992 Amnesty Law to include the period during which the murders were committed. Therefore, amnesty was granted to Bouterse and the other 24 suspects for the 1982 December murders. On 11 May 2012, the military court in charge of the case adjourned the trial of Bouterse until a constitutional court has reviewed the constitutionality of the new Amnesty Law. Desi Bouterse was sentenced on 29 November 2019 to 20 years in prison while he was still president of the country. He was found guilty of planning and ordering the murder of 15 political prisoners on 8 December 1982 at the military barracks of Fort Zeelandia. No arrest warrant has ever been issued in relation to either the charge, the conviction or the sentence. On 22 January 2020 Bouterse started an appeals process against the ruiling. However, after one of the judges fell ill, the case was postponed to 31 March 2020. On 30 August 2021, the Krijgsraad (Highest Court of Suriname) affirmed its 29 November 2019 conviction of Mr. Bouterse, which occurred following a decade-long court martial, and while he was still president. December 2022 will mark 40 years since the extra-judicial killings occurred, as yet without final resolution and justice for the families of those executed.

chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: In April 2008, a military court ruled that all suspects involved in the 1982 December murders had to stand trial, including Bouterse. On 4 April 2012, about two months before the verdict in the trial, the National Assembly passed an amendment to extent the 1992 Amnesty Law to include the period during which the murders were committed. Therefore, amnesty was granted to Bouterse and the other 24 suspects for the 1982 December murders. The amnesty law was revoked in 2016 and the trials continued. In March a military court reinstated the suspension of the case against one defendant ordered by an appellate court in January 2014. In September another of the defendants died of natural causes, reducing the total number of defendants again to 23. During the year, there were several hearings in the case, and in late November the Court of Justice lifted the three-year suspension and ordered the trial against all 23 remaining defendants to continue. As of 2016, three codefendants had died before appearing before the court which is why the court martial decided to dismiss the case against the three deceased codefendants during this year. On November 29 of 2019, seven co-defendants including President Bouterse were found guilty for the extrajudicial killing of 15 political opponents. Three defendants received 15-year prison sentences, and three other defendants received 10-year sentences. Bouterse and four others convicted stated they would appeal their verdicts. One defendant facing a 20-year sentence was acquitted along with nine others whom the prosecution had recommended for acquittal. Six defendants died during the trial process, which started in 2007.

trialRelevantInfo: Klickovic formerly served as the Bosnian Serb prime minister from 1996-1998 and is accused of exerting effective control over the Serb forces, who conducted an attack against Bosniak civilians in Krupa on April 21, 1992. In 1992, Klickovic was president of the wartime Presidency and commander of the Crisis Committee of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa, Drljaca was a member of the Prisoner Exchange Commission in Krupa, and Ostojic was the commander of the 11th Krupa Light Infantry Brigade of the Republika Srpska Army. The three were indicted on August 21, 2008 for exerting effective control over the systemic persecution of non-Serb civilians. On November 5, 2010, the three were acquitted of the war crimes charges because they were not found to have had effective control over those persecuting the civilians. In May 2012, the appeals chamber revoked the first-instance verdict and ordered a retrial of only Klickovic and Drljaca, while clearing Ostojic of all charges. The two were acquitted again in the second-instance verdict on May 7, 2013.

membership: prison or camp guard or correctional officer

However, the statutory limitation period for that offense had elapsed, so CB and MS were acquitted for abuse of authority on January 30, 2012, by the Asti District Court. One of the prison guards, GS, was acquitted because of his lack of involvement in the ill-treatment, and AD and DB were acquitted of the charge of ill-treatment under Article 572 of the Criminal Code because the statute of limitations had expired. The court nonetheless held that the conduct of AD and DB amounted to infliction of bodily harm contrary to Article 582 of the Criminal Code. The trials against the five prison guards were discontinued because of the acquittal sentence for all five defendants.

chargesCategories: maltreatment and excessive use of force
trialRelevantInfo: On June 4, 2014, the Court of Rome convicted nine police officers, Leonardo Mascia, Guido Faggiani, Andrea Serrao, Roberto Marinelli, Adriano Cramerotti, Fabrizio Cola, Leonardo Vinelli, Rossano Bagialemani, and Michele Costanzo, and sentenced them to four years in prison for abuse of power and use of violence against Stefano Gugliotta in 2010. trialRelevantInfo: On March 28, 2016, the Attorney General’s Office announced that General Henry William Torres Escalante and former army commander general Mario Montoya Uribe would be formally charged for their alleged connections to false positive cases. General Montoya faced charges in connection with his alleged involvement in seven false positive cases and awaited arraignment as of mid-October. He was accused of supporting paramilitary groups and actions in operations such as Operation Orion, a 2002 military offensive against guerrillas in Medellin. The Attorney General’s Office reported the investigation of Montoya Uribe was in the preliminary investigation and inquiry phase as of June 2017. Montoya Uribe chose to bring his pending case to the JEP, and on April 25, 2019, the JEP began to review the case against Montoya Uribe for his involvement in false positive killings. While Montoya Uribe was charged in 2016, the investigation had been suspended indefinitely until 2021, when he was charged yet again with over 100 extrajudicial killings, as well as corruption and links to paramilitarism. However, there has been tension between the traditional court system and the JEP over the prosecution of Montoya Uribe. In August 2021, the Superior Court of Bogotá decided on an appeal for reversal of the charges and ruled that only the JEP could file charges against the defendant. It does not appear that the JEP has filed charges yet, and the case against Montoya Uribe is still pending as of June 2022.

trialRelevantInfo: On March 28, 2016, the Attorney General’s Office announced that General Henry William Torres Escalante and former army commander general Mario Montoya Uribe would be formally charged for their alleged connections to false positive cases. Torres Escalante was charged with homicide of a protected person. The attorney general found that General Torres Escalante participated in the homicide of Daniel Torres Arciniegas and his son Roque Julio Torres, who were falsely presented as FARC members killed in combat in 2007. On March 28, 2016, authorities arrested Torres Escalante, which marked the first instance an active-duty general faced criminal charges related to the false positives scandal. He was called to trial in August. The case against Torres Escalante was transferred to the special investigations unit in 2016, after a court upheld his indictment. On August 4, 2017, Torres Escalante was granted conditional liberty under the transitional justice mechanism of the peace accord. However, in December 2017, the Superior Court of Yopal revoked his conditional liberty and ordered that he be rearrested. The court held that conditional liberty could only be granted once the Special Jurisdiction for Peace was operational (Escalante Torres had brought his case to the JEP). On July 10, 2018, the JEP began to review the case against Torres Escalante. On July 25, 2020, Torres Escalante admitted his responsibility for false positives before the JEP and apologized to the families of the victims. Despite admitting his guilt by omission, the JEP denied to release him early.

charges: Beating and murder of Sandro Girgvliani
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted; illegal imprisonment; maltreatment and excessive use of force
trialRelevantInfo: In July 2006 four Ministry of Internal Affairs officers were convicted by the Tbilisi City Court in the January beating death of Sandro Girgvliani and sentenced to prison terms of from seven to eight years. The officers appealed to the Supreme Court after the trial court's decision was upheld by the Tbilisi Court of Appeals in December 2006. In July 2007 the Supreme Court removed six months from the final sentences for all four defendants, based on changes to the law regarding destruction of property, one of the charges against the officers. Many observers believed that senior ministry officials ordered his beating. The officers were Gia Alania, chief of the first unit of the ministry’s department of constitutional security, and three of his subordinates, Avtandil Aptsiauri, Aleksandre Gachava, and Mikheil Bibiluri. They only served three years in prison as a result of a presidential pardon in November 2008.

chargesCategories: torture; other
trialRelevantInfo: In January 2014 the Prosecutor General’s Office charged Bachana “Bacho” Akhalaia, who formerly held posts as minister of internal affairs (2012), of defense (2009- 12), and of corrections (2005-08), and Megis Kardava, former head of the military police department and former director of Prison No. 7, with torture and exceeding official powers in the so-called Navtlughi special operations. Prosecutors alleged the defendants participated in beating six prisoners to extract confessions for an investigation into an attempted escape from Prison No. 1 in Rustavi. In October the courts found both Davit Akhalaia and Megis Kardava guilty as charged and sentenced them to 10 years in prison. The court also found two other former interior ministry officials, Levan Kardava and Giorgi Mazmishvili, guilty of the premeditated murder of three persons in the same operation and sentenced them each to 11 years in prison. As of November the case continued against Davit Akhalaia, the former head of the constitutional protection department, and Giorgi Dgebuadze, the former head of one of the department’s units, regarding their role in the operation. On February 27, 2018, the Tbilisi Court of Appeals upheld former deputy defense minister Davit Akhalaia’s 2016 conviction for conspiracy to commit murder and abuse of power during the 2006 Navtlughi special operation that resulted in the killing of three unarmed men. In April 2018, the Tbilisi City Court convicted former defense minister Bacho Akhalaia of organizing torture and sexual violence to 12 years in prison (in absentia). It also convicted Giorgi Dgebuadze to nine years. On 19 October 2018, the Georgian Supreme Court confirmed these sentences.

trialRelevantInfo: Iraqi-Bosnian businessman Abduladhim Maktouf was first arrested in June 2004 in BiH on suspicion of economic crimes, but following investigation, was later indicted for war crimes associated with the Al Mujahid armed group of the Army of BiH. On July 1, 2005, the Trial panel of the Court of BiH convicted Maktouf of war crimes against civilians and sentenced him to 5 years in prison, the minimum mandatory sentence for such crimes. The verdict was appealed, and the appeals chamber ordered a retrial. On April 4, 2006, the appeals panel convicted Maktouf again and sentenced him to 5 years in prison. In 2013, Bosnia began released previously convicted war criminals, including Maktouf, because the Bosnian criminal code was improperly used, rather than the criminal code of the former Yugoslavia. The release and re-trying of these convicts was supported and encouraged by the European Court for Human Rights. Maktouf was re-tried in July 2014, and on July 11, 2014, the Bosnian state court sentenced Maktouf to 5 years in prison under the criminal code of the former Yugoslavia. The defense appealed, and on March 17, 2015, the Appeals chamber reduced Maktouf’s sentence from 5 years to 3 years in prison. On November 9, 2016, the Bosnian state court awarded Maktouf €36,600 in compensation for serving a sentence that was 2 years longer than it should have been.

trialRelevantInfo: Kosovo Serbs Miroslav Vuckovic and Bozur Bisevac were first indicted in November 1999 for genocide of Albanian civilians from March 22, 1999 to early May 1999 in the Mitrovica municipality. The two are accused of setting fire to residences, forced displacement, confiscation of private property, and murder of an elderly villager by arson. The trial began in June 2000. Bisevac escaped detention in August 2000, and UNMIK regulations prohibited prosecution of suspects in absentia, so the court abandoned the prosecution of Bisevac in January 2001. On January 18, 2001, the District Court of Mitrovica convicted Vuckovic of genocide, sentencing him to 14 years in prison. The defense appealed, and on April 9, 2001, the Supreme Court revoked the verdict and ordered a re-trial. The Supreme Court judges commented that deportation of Kosovo-Albanians was a formal policy under the Milosevic regime, so the deportation and forcible transfer of these civilians should not be considered genocide. The re-trial in the Mitrovica District Court began in January 2002 under the amended indictment alleging war crimes against civilians, and on May 23, 2008, the international panel of judges of the Mitrovica District Court, presided by International Judge Lolita Dumlao, convicted Vuckovic of war crimes against civilians under the criminal code of the former Yugoslavia and sentenced him to 8 years in prison. By May 2008, Vuckovic had also been sentenced to 5 years in prison for burning and looting of civilians’ houses, as well as 7 years for violence and arson, committed on April 15, 1999 in the village of Gushac.

trialRelevantInfo: Bosnian Croat former commander of the Kaonik prison Zlatko Aleksovski was indicted on November 10, 1995 for outrages upon personal dignity towards non-Croat civilians from January to May 1993. Aleksovski was originally indicted alongside Dario Kordic, Mario Cerkez, Tihomir Blaskic, Ivan Santic, and Paro Skopljak, but the indictments against Santic and Skopljak were soon withdrawn, and the trials of Blaskic, Kordic, and Cerkez were separated. Aleksovski is accused of subjecting approximately 500 non-Croat prisoners to physical and psychological maltreatment as well as violent acts. Aleksovski was indicted on November 10, 1995, arrested and detained on June 8, 1996 by Croatian authorities, and his case was transferred to the ICTY on April 28, 1997. On May 7, 1999, the ICTY trial chamber sentenced Aleksovski to 2.5 years in prison, with credit to time served in detention. The counsel for the prosecution in the trial chamber was Grant Niemann and Anura Meddegoda. The verdict was appealed by both parties, and on March 24, 2000, the appeals chamber increased Aleksovski’s guilty sentence to 7 years imprisonment. The counsel for the prosecution in the appeals chamber was Upswana Yapa and Anura Meddegoda. Aleksovski was transferred to Finland to serve the remainder of his sentence on September 22, 2000, and was granted early release on November 14, 2001.

trialRelevantInfo: During the Balkan wars, Bosnian Serb Vidoje Blagojevic was a Colonel in command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade with the Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), and Bosnian Serb Dragan Jokic was a Major acting as Chief of Engineering off the Zvornik Brigade, as well as advisor to the Zvornik Brigade Commander and to the Deputy Commander of the Bosnian Serb army (VRS). Blagojevic and Jokic are charged with individual criminal responsibility for participating in a joint criminal enterprise with the common purpose of persecution of Bosniak Muslim civilians. After several amendments beginning in 1998, indictments of Blagojevic and Jokic for crimes against humanity were joined together in 2003, and trial proceedings against the two commenced on May 14, 2003. On January 17, 2005, the trial chamber issued its judgement decision. Blagojevic was found not guilty of extermination, but was convicted of genocide (complicity to genocide by aiding and abetting genocide), crimes against humanity (aiding and abetting murder, persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds, and inhumane acts by forcible transfer), and violations of the customs of war (aiding and abetting murder), and was sentenced to 18 years in prison. Jokic was acquitted of murder as a crime against humanity, but was convicted of crimes against humanity (aiding and abetting extermination and persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds) and violations of the customs of war (aiding and abetting murder) and was sentenced to 9 years in prison. Both defendants appealed, and on May 9, 2007, the appeals chamber reduced Blagojevic’s sentence to 15 years, reversing his conviction for complicity in genocide, and affirmed Jokic’s 9 year sentence. Blagojevic was transferred to Norway to serve his sentence in 2008, and was granted early release by the President of the International Tribunal on February 3, 2012 and was released in December that same year. Jokic was transferred to Austria to serve his sentence in 2008, and was granted early release on January 13, 2010.
