trialRelevantInfo: Bosnian Serb Radoslav Brdanin was a leading political figure in the Autonomous Region of Krajina and government of the Republika Srpska during the armed conflict in the region between Serb forces and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defense Council. Brdanin was first indicted in 1999, though this indictment was amended six times until 2003. Brdanin was arrested and quickly transferred to the ICTY in 1999 by the NATO-led Stabilization Force of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On September 1, 2004, the trial chamber convicted Brdanin of crimes against humanity (persecutions, torture, deportation, inhumane acts, forcible transfer), violations of the law or customs of war (wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages not justified by military necessity, destruction or willful damage to religious instititions), and grave breaches of the Geneva conventions (willful killing, torture) and was sentenced to 32 years in prison. Brdanin was acquitted of all other counts. Both the prosecution and defense appealed, and on April 3, 2007, the appeals chamber reversed some convictions and reduced Brdanin’s sentence to 30 years. Brdanin was transferred to Denmark to serve the remainder of his sentence in March 2008.

charges: Crimes against humanity including persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; other; crimes against humanity
trialRelevantInfo: Miroslav Deronjic, former political leader of the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, used his authority to give orders to the Bratunac Territorial Defense to attack the village of Glogova, resulting in the death of 65 Bosnian Muslim civilians on May 9, 1992. Deronjic is also accused of exercising his superiority to persecute and systemically attack the Bosnian Muslim civilian population during his time as President of the Bratunac crisis staff. He was first indicted for charges of crimes against humanity in July of 2002, then was quickly arrested by the multinational NATO-run stabilization force (SFOR) and was transferred to the ICTY to face trial. Deronjic pleaded guilty to persecution charges on September 30, 2003, and on March 30, 2004, the trial chamber convicted him of crimes against humanity including persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds and sentenced him to 10 years in prison. Deronjic filed an appeal against his sentence, but his sentence was affirmed by the appeals chamber on July 20, 2005. Deronjic was transferred to Sweden to serve the remainder of his sentence in November 2005, and passed away in detention on May 19, 2007.

trialRelevantInfo: Drazen Erdemovic, former soldier in the 10 Sabotage Detachment of the Bosnian Serb Army (VRS), participated, as part of a firing squad, in the unlawful killing of hundreds of unarmed Bosnian Muslim men, as well as personally killed about 70 civilians during armed conflict around July 16, 1995. Erdemovic was first arrested in March 1996 by authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was indicted in May 1996, and was immediately transferred to the ICTY to face trial. Erdemovic was charged with murder as both a crime against humanity as well as murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. At his initial appearance, Erdemovic pleaded guilty to the count of murder as a crime against humanity, and the trial chamber dismissed the alternative count. On November 29, 1996, the trial chamber convicted Erdemovic of crimes against humanity and sentenced him to 10 years in prison. Erdemovic’s defense appealed the sentence, asking the appeals chamber to revise the verdict to read guilty as charged, and excuse him from serving the sentence, claiming he committed these crimes under duress. trialRelevantInfo: Bosnian Croat forces (HVO) and Bosnian Muslim forces (ABiH) engaged in armed conflict throughout central Bosnia in 1992 and 1993. Mario Cerkez was Commander of the Vitez Brigade of the HVO during the armed conflict. Kordic and Cerkez were indicted in November 1995 before surrendering in October 1997 and immediately being transferred to the ICTY to face war crimes charges. Both plead not guilty to all charges, and on February 26, 2001, the trial chamber convicted both Kordic and Cerkez on the basis of individual criminal responsibility of war crimes. Kordic was convicted of grave breaches of the Geneva conventions (Willful killing; inhuman treatment; unlawful confinement of civilians), violations of the laws or customs of war (Unlawful attack on civilians; unlawful attack on civilian objects; wanton destruction not justified by military necessity; plunder of public or private property; destruction or willful damage to institutions dedicated to religion or education), and crimes against humanity (Persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds; murder; inhumane acts; imprisonment) and was sentenced to 25 years in prison. Cerkez was convicted of crimes against humanity (Persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds, murder, inhumane acts, imprisonment), grave breaches of the Geneva conventions (Wilful killing; inhuman treatment; unlawful confinement of civilians; taking civilians as hostages) and violations of the laws or customs of war (Unlawful attack on civilians; unlawful attack on civilian objects; wanton destruction not justified by military necessity; plunder of public or private property; destruction or willful damage to institutions dedicated to religion or education) and was sentenced to 15 years in prison. Krajisnik was arrested and immediately transferred to the ICTY in April 2000 to face trial for war crimes charges. Krajisnik pleaded not guilty to all charges, and on September 27, 2006, the trial chamber convicted him of crimes against humanity (persecutions, murder, extermination, deportation, forced transfer) and acquitted him of genocide and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Krajisnik was sentenced to 27 years in prison. Both the defense and prosecution appealed, and on March 17, 2009, the appeals chamber reduced Krajisnik’s sentence to 20 years in prison. Krajisnik was transferred to the UK to serve his sentence in September 2009, and was granted early release in August 2013.

trialRelevantInfo: In April of 1993, Bosnian Croat forces (HVO) engaged in an unlawful attack against Bosnian Muslim civilian inhabitants of the small village of Ahmici in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bala was transferred to France to serve the remainder of this sentence in May 2008, and was granted early release in June 2012.

trialRelevantInfo: Former Bosnian Serb paramilitary members Milan Lukić and Sredoje Lukić were first indicted for war crimes charges in October 1998 for their role in the cruel treatment and murder of Bosnian Muslin civilians between June 7, 1992 and October 10, 1994. Sredoje Lukic was convicted of crimes against humanity (inhumane acts, murder, aiding and abetting persecutions and inhumane acts) and violations of the laws or customs of war (cruel treatment, murder, aiding and abetting cruel treatment) and was sentenced to 30 years in prison. All parties appealed, and on December 4, 2012, the appeal chamber upheld Milan Lukic’s sentence and reduced Sredoje Lukic’s sentence to 27 years in prison. Milan Lukic was transferred to Estonia to serve his sentence in February 2014, and Sredoje Lukic was transferred to Norway in August 2013.

trialRelevantInfo: Zdravko Mucić, Hazim Delic, Esad Landžo, and Zejnil Delalić were indicted in March 1996 for the cruel and oppressive acts against Serb detainees in the Čelebići prison camp near Konjic, central Bosnia and Herzegovina from March until December 1992. During this time, Mucic was commander of the Čelebići prison camp, Delic was deputy commander of the camp, Landzo was a guard at the camp, and Delalic was coordinator of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces in the Knojic area as well as commander of the First Tactical Group of the Bosnian Army. Mucic was arrested by Austrian authorities in March 1996 and extradited to the ICTY, Delic and Landzo were arrested by Bosnian authorities in May 1996 and extradited to the ICTY, and Delalic was arrested by German authorities in March 1996 and extradited to the ICTY. All four defendants pleaded not guilty to all charges, and their trial began in March 1997. On November 16, 1998, the trial chamber acquitted Delalic of all charges and convicted Mucic, Delic, and Landzo of grave breaches of the Geneva conventions (willful killings, willfully causing great suffering or injury, inhuman treatment, unlawful confinement of civilians) and violations of the laws or customs of war (murders, torture, cruel treatment) and sentenced them to 7, 20, and 15 years in prison, respectively. All parties appealed, and on February 20, 2001, the appeals chamber confirmed the acquittal of Delalic and ordered a retrial for the other three accused. After the second trial, on October 9, 2001, the new trial chamber sentenced Mucic, Delic, and Landzo to 9, 18, and 15 years in prison, respectively. This third-instance verdict was appealed, and on April 8, 2003, the appeals chamber upheld the third instance verdict handed down by Trial Chamber II. In July 2003, Mucic was granted early release, and Delic and Landzo were transferred to Finland to serve their sentences. Landzo was granted early release in April 2006, and Delic was granted early release in June 2008.

name: Cedomir Jovanovic
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Cedomir Jovanovic and Andjelko Kolasinac and the 6 others were indicted in August 2000 for war crimes due to aiding and assisting armed forces who attacked civilians in Orahovac, Kosovo in 1998-1999. Kolasinac was the mayor of Kosovo during the armed conflict period, and Jovanovic was a member of a paramilitary group. Nenad Matic, Vakoslav Simic, Arsenije Vitoshevic, Stanislav Levic, Radosav Misic, and Novica Krsic escaped custody, leaving only Jovanovic and Kolasinac to face trial. In June 2001, a court with international judges convicted both defendants and Jovanovic was given 20 years in prison while Kolasinac was given a 5 year sentence. Jovanovic was convicted as charged with war crimes against civilians, and Kolasinac was convicted of Giving Help to the Offender after the Commission of a Criminal Act. The judgement was heavily criticized by human rights monitors for the lack of due process, as the trial was conducted in a language not native to the defendants, and they could not follow their own trial. The decision was appealed, and on November 2, 2001, the sentence for Jovanovic was affirmed, but a re-trial for Kolasinac was ordered. On January 31, 2003, the trial panel of the Prizren District Court convicted Kolasinac of three counts of war crimes against civilians including forced displacement, deportation, and forced labor, and sentenced him to 8 years in prison. The decision was appealed again, and on August 5, 2004, the Supreme Court overturned the first instance verdict and ordered a re-trial.

On May 30, 2002, a majority international trial panel decided not to re-try Ajeti in absentia. The panel began the re-trial of Stojanovic independently. No updates on the outcome of the trial have been found.

name: Naim Kadriu
position_desc: former member of the Kosovo Liberation Army
position_desc_fr: ancien membre de l'Armée de libération du Kosovo
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; torture; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Kosovo Albanians Latif Gashi, Nazif Mehmeti, Naim Kadriu, and Rrustem Mustafa were indicted in February 2003 for war crimes against civilians committed between March 24 and June 12, 1999 in Kosovo. During this time, Gashi was a Commander, and the others were general members of the KLA. On July 16, 2003, the District Court of Pristina convicted Gashi, Mehmeti, Kadriu, and Mustafa and sentenced them to 10, 13, 5, and 17 years in prison, respectively. The decision was appealed, and on July 21, 2005, the Kosovo Supreme Court sent the case back for re-trial. Naim Kadriu died before the re-trial began. On October 2, 2009, the District Court of Pristina convicted Gashi, Mehmeti, and Mustafa and sentenced them to 6, 3, and 4 years in prison. On January 26, 2011, the Supreme Court partially upheld the previous verdict, but sent the case back for a second re-trial with regards to count 8 of the indictment. On June 7, the Basic Court of Pristina convicted Gashi, Mehmeti, and Mustafa of war crimes against civilians and sentenced them to 6, 3, and 4 years in prison, respectively. The defense attempted to appeal the sentences, but the appeals were dismissed as unfounded by the Supreme Court of Kosovo on May 13, 2016 and the previous decision was upheld.

name: Riza “Commander Hoxha” Alija
position_desc: former member of the Kosovo Liberation Army
position_desc_fr: ancien membre de l'Armée de libération du Kosovo
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Former KLA members Sabit Geci, Riza Alija, Haki Hajdari, and Shaban Hoti were indicted in November 2010 for war crimes against civilians from May 18 until June 3, 1999 during the armed conflict in Kosovo. During this time, Geci held a command position in the improvised prison within a KLA military compound, Alija, Hajdari, Rexhepi, and Hoti were unranked KLA members. Trial proceedings against Sali Rexhepi were terminated when he left the country to fly to Turkey for urgently needed heart surgery. The trial of the other four defendants proceeded. On July 29, 2011, the District Court of Mitrovica convicted Geci of four counts of war crimes against civilians and one count of unauthorized weapons possession and sentenced him to 15 years, convicted Alija of two counts of war crimes against civilians and sentenced him to 12 years, and convicted Hajdari and Hoti of one count of war crimes against civilians and sentenced them to 6 and 7 years in prison, respectively. Sali Rexhepi was tried and convicted of war crimes in his own independent trial, which was re-joined with the other four defendants after their first instance decision during appeals proceedings. On September 11, 2013, the Court of Appeals of Kosovo upheld the sentence for Geci, Hajdari, Hoti, and Rexhepi, and extended Alija’s sentence to 12 years.

chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; torture; other; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Former KLA members Syleman Selimi, Sami Lushtaku, Jahir Demaku, Sabit Geci, Ismet Haxha, Sahit Jashari and Avni Zabeli were arrested in May 2013 on suspicion of having committed war crimes against civilians during armed conflict in 1998. The defendants are accused of beating civilian men who were detained at a KLA detention center. The arrests provoked protests from those in support of the Kosovo Liberation Army, who demanded the release of the defendants. On May 27, 2015, the Basic Court of Mitrovica released their judgment. Sylejman Selimi was convicted of murder and sentenced to 6 years in prison. Sami Lushtaku was convicted of torturing a civlian prisoner and was sentenced to 12 years in prison. The court acquitted Sahit Jashari, Ismet Haxha, Avni Zabeli, Jahir Demaku, and Sabit Geci. On October 25, 2016, the Appellate Court adjusted Selimi’s conviction to 6 years and 3 months in prison, revised Lushtaku’s sentence to 7 year for war crimes against civilians, and upheld the acquittals of Sahit Jashari, Ismet Haxha, Avni Zabeli, Jahir Demaku, and Sabit Geci. Selimi is the former ambassador to Albania, and Lushtaku was the serving mayor at the time the trial began. The decision was appealed again, and on July 3, 2017, the Supreme Court acquitted Lushtaku of all charges.

name: Slobodan Martinovic
charges: War crimes against civilians (inhumane treatment, illegal detention in inhumane conditions)
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; illegal imprisonment; other; maltreatment and excessive use of force; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Kosovo Serbs Slobodan Martinovic, Srecko Martinovic, and Svetlana Sojanovic were arrested in September 2009 by EULEX police on suspicion of having committed war crimes in 1999. At this time, Slobodan Martinovic was a former army driver, Srecko Martinovic was a Yugoslav Army cook, and Sojanovic was a civilian. The three were indicted in April 2011 and accused of kidnapping and torturing eight people in a detention center. near Novoberde/Novo Brdo and Gjilan/Gnjilane. On July 22, 2011, the three defendants were acquitted by the District Court of Pristina. The decision was appealed, and on July 25, 2013, the EULEX Trial Chamber of the Court of Appeals in Pristina revoked the first-instance verdict and ordered a re-trial. The re-trial took place, and on November 7, 2014, the District Court of Pristina acquitted the defendants of all charges. The prosecution appealed, but on October 2, 2015, the Court of Appeals rejected the appeal and affirmed the first instance judgment. The chief state prosecutor then filed for a protection of legality, which was approved on July 29, 2016.

name: Agush Memishi
position_desc: former member of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) Gjilane Group
position_desc_fr: ancien membre du groupe de Gjilane de l'Armée de libération du Kosovo (UCK)
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; torture
trialRelevantInfo: Former members of the KLA Gnjilane Group Agush Memishi, Samet Hajdari, Nazif Hasani, Ahmet Hasani, Burin Fazli, Selimon Sadiki, Faton Hajdari, Ferat Hajdari, Kamber Sahiti, Sadik Aliu, Shefqet Musliu, Fazli Ajdari, Rexhep Aliu, Shaqir Shaqiri, Idriz Aliu, Ramadan Halimi, and Shemsi Nuhui are accused of war crimes against civilians, including the repeated rape and abuse of two Kosovo Serb women.On January 21, 2011, a court in Belgrade convicted nine members of the Gjilane Group and sentenced them to a total of 101 years in prison. The court cleared charges against Fazli Ajdari, Rexhep Aliu, Shaqir Shaqiri, Idriz Aliu, Ramadan Halimi, and Shemsi Nuhui, who had been extradited from Serbia in May 2012 to face trial. Agush Memishi was sentenced to 12 years, Samet Hajdari to 15, Nazif Hasani and Ahmet Hasani to 13 years in prison each. Burim Fazli and Selimon Sadiki to 12 years, Faton Hajdari to 10, Ferat Hajdari, Kamber Sahiti and Sadik Aliu to eight years each, and Shefqet Musliu to five years of prison.

name: Shefket Musliu
charges: Kidnapping of four persons, attempted extortion, unauthoritzed possession of weapons (acquitted), and criminal association (acquitted)
chargesCategories: other; illegal imprisonment
trialRelevantInfo: Shefket Musliu, Besim Tahiri, Jeton Arifi, Feriz Qerimi, and Xhevedet Musliu were indicted in December 2003 for kidnapping, attempted extortion, illegal possession of firearms, and criminal association. The defendants are accused of committing these acts in September 2001. On June 25, 2004, the District Court in Gjilan/Gnjilan acquitted Jeton Arifi and Xhevdet Musliu and convicted the other three defendants, sentencing Shefket Musliu, Tahiri, and Qerimi to 12, 7, and 5 years in prison, respectively. A new hearing was launched against Musliu and Tahiri, as Qerimi died in the meantime. On October 5, 2010, the District Court in Gjilan sentenced Musliu and Tahiri to 10.5 and 6.75 years in prison, respectively.

name: Frank Ronghi
position_desc: US Soldier on NATO peacekeeping mission in Kosovo
position_desc_fr: Soldat américain en mission de maintien de la paix de l'OTAN au Kosovo
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted; other
trialRelevantInfo: Frank Ronghi, a U.S. soldier who was on a peacekeeping mission in Kosovo, was arrested in Kosovo after the body of 11-year-old girl Marita Shabiu was discovered in January 2000. Ronghi was in Kosovo as part of a NATO peacekeeping mission, and specifically was part of the Third Battalion of the 504th parachute Infantry. The defendant was accused of sodomozing and murdering Merita in an abandoned building in Vitina before stuffing her body in a plastic bag and dumping it in the woods. Ronghi pleaded guilty to the charges of murder, forcible sodomy, and indecent acts. On August 2, 2000, a US Military Court in Germany sentenced Ronghi to life in prison without the possibility of parole for his crimes. In addition to the sentence, Ronghi was dishonorably discharged and was handed a rank reduction. Ronghi was sent to Kosovo from Fort Bragg, and was confined to Wuerzburg military prison, 60 miles east of Frankfurt.

name: Ilir Rrecaj
position_desc: Former official from the Ministry of Health
position_desc_fr: Ancien fonctionnaire du ministère de la santé
chargesCategories: other; maltreatment and excessive use of force
trialRelevantInfo: Investigations about a human organ-trafficking ring began in 2008 when a Kosovo clinic was raided by police after a man collapsed while waiting for a flight after having his kidney removed. The Medicus clinic had illegally removed at least 30 kidneys in 2008 and gave donors incentive payments of 15,000 euros/$A19,000, while recipients would pay up to 100,000 for organs bought from the clinic. In 2008, Rrecaj was a former official from the health ministry, Lufti and Arban Dervishi were Kosovar doctors, Sonmez was a Turkish doctor, and Harel was an Israeli citizen. The trial began in 2011 and was managed by EULEX judges. On April 30, 2013, a EULEX-run court in Kosovo acquitted Rrecaj, and convicted the other doctors, sentencing Lufti Dervishi to 8 years, Arban Dervishi to 7 years 3 months, and the other three doctors received terms between 1 and 3 years in prison.

name: Agron Ibrahimi
charges: Participating in a group that killed a civilian, inflicted serious bodily injury on his mother, and considerably damaged at least one house and one car, aggravated murder
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted; other
trialRelevantInfo: Kosovo Albanians Agron Ibrahimi, Nexhat Ramadani, Saqip Brahimi, Xheladin Salihu, Sadri Shabani, and Agim Abdullah were indicted in September 2004 for charges of aggravated murder, two counts of causing general danger, two counts of participating in a group that commits a criminal act, and Salihu was additionally charged with illegal weapons possession. The indictment alleges that the six defendants were responsible for a murder of a civilian and serious injury suffered by his mother on March 17, 2004. On May 19, 2005, all six defendants were convicted of participating in a group that killed a civilian, inflicted serious bodily injury on his mother, and considerably damaged at least one house and one car. Ramadani was additionally convicted of aggravated murder, and Xheladin Salihu was additionally convicted of assisting aggravated murder and illegal possession of a weapon. The defendants were acquitted of all remaining charges. Ibrahimi was sentenced to 2.5 years in prison, Ramadani was sentenced to 16 years, Brahimi was given 3.5 years, Salihu was given 11 years, Shabani and Abdullah were given 2.5 years. The decision was appealed by all parties except Brahimi, and on June 23, 2009, the Supreme Court of Kosovo largely upheld the first instance verdict, but additionally acquitted Salihu of the charge of assisting aggravated murder and reduced his sentence to 2 years and 7 months. Though this case did not take place during a civil war, it will be coded as an instance of conflict transitional justice, because the instance involves groups that were in conflict during the war in 1999.

With the establishment of the PGoK, Krasniqi became the PGoK spokesperson. All four were arrested by the Special Prosecutor and transferred to the detention facilities of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in the Hague in November 2020 shortly after their indictment. The defendants pleaded not guilty to the charges, and when an amended indictment was filed in April 2022, they maintained their plea of innocence. The trial is ongoing.

name: Danilo Tešić

position_desc_fr: Soldat de l'armée yougoslave (VJ) du 1er peloton de fusiliers
chargesCategories: murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: According to an indictment filed in September 2002, Former Yugoslav Army soldiers Danilo Tesic, Misel Seregi, Zlatko Mancic, Rade Radojevic are accused of killing two ethnic Albanians during the war in Kosovo in 1999. At this time, Mancic was a commanding security officer, Radojevic was Commander of the 1st Rifle Platoon of the VJ 549th Motorised Brigade, and Tesic and Seregi were soldiers of the 1st Rifle Platoon. On October 11, 2002, the Nis Military Court Tesic and Seregi of physically committing the killings, and Mancic and Radojevic for authorizing the killings. Tesic was given 4 years, Seregi was given 3 years, Mancic was given 7 years, and Radojevic was given 5 years. The decision was appealed, and in May 2003, the Supreme Court in Belgrade, which had jurisdiction to hear appeals, increased Tesic’s sentence to 7 years, Seregi’s sentence to 5 years, Mancic’s sentence to 14 years, and Radojevic’s sentence to 9 years. The sentence was appealed again, and in November 2005, the Supreme Court of Serbia quashed the judgment and sent the case back for retrial. The retrial began in June 2007 before the District Court in Nis, then was transferred to the Chamber of the Higher Court in Nis in 2010. In August 2012, the High Court in Nis convicted Tesic, Seregi, Mancic, and Radojevic, and sentenced them to 7, 5, 12, and 9 years, respectively.

trialRelevantInfo: Trials proceedings against Milorad “Legija Lukovic” Ulemek were launched in 2004 for the murder of former Serbian president Ivan Stambolic in 2000. Stambolic was kidnapped in August 2000 in a Belgrade park, killed with a shot to the back of the head, and dumped in a shallow pit in a forest in Fruska Gora, Serbia. The trial also accuses the defendants of attempting to assassinate Vuk Draskovic on June 15, 2000. At the time of the murders, Lukovic was a paramilitary commander of Special Operations under Slobodan Milosevic. Rade Markovic was the Milosevic-era secret service chief. Bracanovic was the deputy chief of the Security Information Agency. The others were members of the Special Operations unit. On July 18, 2005, the Special Court in Belgrade rendered its judgment. Milorad Lukovic was convicted of murder and attempted murder and given 40 years, Markovic was given 15 years, Maricic, Bujosevic, and Bercek were given 40 years, Milivojevic and Ilic were given 15 years, and Bracanovic was given four years for trying to cover up the crime. All defendants were already serving prison terms for separate convictions. The verdict was appealed, and on June 14, 2006, the Supreme Court of Serbia upheld the first instance verdict.

charges: Massacre of 200 Croatian prisoners of war
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: Former members of the Vukovar Territorial Defense of the Yugoslav People’s Army were accused of responsibility for the massacre of around 200 Croatian prisoners of war in Ovcara, Croatia. The massacre took place on November 20, 1991 at the Ovcara farm and the Vukovar hospital in Croatia during the armed conflict with Serb military forces. At the time of the crime, Miroljub Vujovic was a Vukovar Territorial Defense Commander, Stanko Vujanovic was his deputy, Milan Lancuzanin was commander of the Leva Supoderica volunteer unit, and the others were soldiers. The accused were indicted in September 2005. Trial proceedings against Sosic were suspended as he passed away while awaiting trial. On December 12, 2005, the War Crimes Chamber of the District Court in Belgrade convicted 12 remaining defendants, and acquitted Ljuboja and Katic. Vujovic, Vujanovic, Milojevic, Atanasijevic, Djankovic, and Radak were given 20 year sentences, Kalaba was given 9 years, Madzarac was given 12 years, and Mugosa was given 5 years. Vojnovic, Peric, Lancuzanin, and Dragovic were given sentences of some unknown length. Sasa Radak was tried separately in his first-instance trial, and was convicted and received a 20-year sentence. On October 18, 2006, the Supreme Court of Serbia nullified the first instance verdict and sent the case back for retrial due to a violation of criminal procedure. The court also overturned Radak’s verdict, and merged the two trials. A new verdict for the re-trial was handed down by the War Crimes Trial Chamber of the Belgrade District Court on March 12, 2009, but was not published until 2017. In the retrial, Vojnovic, Peric, Lancuzcanin, Dragovic, Zlatar, Madzarac, Ljuboja, and Katic were acquitted; sentences were upheld for Vujovic, Vujanovic, Milojevic, and Mugosa; sentences were decreased to 15 years for Atanasijevic and 5 years for Djankovic and Radak; and increased to 11 years for Kalaba.

The Scorpions unit was under command of the Republika Srpska army and Srpska Krajina army. At the time of the crime, Slobodan was the chief of the Scorpions unit, Pero Petrasevic was his bodyguard, and the others were members of the unit. Pero Petrasevic pleaded guilty, claiming his commander, Slobodan Medic, had given the order and he had to choose between carrying out the order or being killed himself. On April 10, 2007, the Special War Crimes Chamber in Belgrade rendered its judgment. Slobodan Medic and Branislav medic received 20 year sentences, Petrasevic received 13 years, Aleksander Medic received 5 years, and Aleksander Vukov was acquitted due to lack of evidence.

trialRelevantInfo: Milorad Lazic, Perica Djakovic, Nikola “Vujina” Vujnovic, Mirko Marunic, Nikola “Sisak” Konjevic, and Savo Kupresanin were indicted in October 1996 in Croatia for war crimes committed during armed conflict in the town of Medek in 1991. At this time, the accused were members of the Republic of Serbian Krajina statelet’s police forces and the Yugoslav People’s Army. On October 10, 2000, the County Court of Gospicu in Croatia convicted Lazic, Djakovic, Vujnovic, Marunic, and Konjevic of war crimes against prisoners of war. Lazic, Djakovic, and Konjevic received 8 year sentences, while Vujnovic and Marunic received 6 year sentences. Kupresanin was acquitted. The decision was appealed, but the Republic of Croatia Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded and upheld the first instance decision on October 26, 2000. A retrial commenced in May 2011, on July 1, 2011, the Higher Court in Belgrade again acquitted Djakovic.

chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; war crimes
trialRelevantInfo: Milorad Lazic, Perica Djakovic, Nikola “Vujina” Vujnovic, Mirko Marunic, Nikola “Sisak” Konjevic, and Savo Kupresanin were indicted in October 1996 in Croatia for war crimes committed during armed conflict in the town of Medek in 1991. At this time, the accused were members of the Republic of Serbian Krajina statelet’s police forces and the Yugoslav People’s Army. On October 10, 2000, the County Court of Gospicu in Croatia convicted Lazic, Djakovic, Vujnovic, Marunic, and Konjevic of war crimes against prisoners of war. Lazic, Djakovic, and Konjevic received 8 year sentences, while Vujnovic and Marunic received 6 year sentences. Kupresanin was acquitted. The decision was appealed, but the Republic of Croatia Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded and upheld the first instance decision on October 26, 2000. The State Attorney’s Office of the Republic of Croatia transferred this case, known as the Medak case, to the Office of the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor, who issued an indictment in October 2009. The indictment was amended on June 7, 2010 to withdraw charges against Vujnovic after witnesses provided an alibi for the defendant. On June 23, 2010, the War Crimes Chamber of the Higher Court in Belgrade acquitted Djakovic and sentenced Lazic and Konjevic to 3 years in prison and Marunic to 2 years in prison.On January 19, 2011, the Court of Appeal in Belgrade rejected the appeals as unfounded and upheld the first instance decision with regards to the convicted defendants, but overturned the acquittal of Djakovic and sent his case back for re-trial. A retrial commenced in May 2011, on July 1, 2011, the Higher Court in Belgrade again acquitted Djakovic.

trialRelevantInfo: Nedeljko Milidragovic, Aleksa Golijanin, Milivoje Batinica, Aleksandar Dacevic, Bora Miletic, Jovan Petrovic, Vidoslav Vasic, and Dragomir Parovic were indicted for their alleged involvement in the capture and killing of about 1,300 Bosnian Muslims near Srebrenica in July 1995 in BiH. At the time of the massacre, the accused were members of the Republika Srpska Interior Ministry’s Special Police Brigade. The defendants were detained in 2015, but later released and walked freely despite the grave charges they faced. The trial of the accused commenced at the War Crimes Chamber in the Belgrade Court in December 2016, and hearings were postponed several times over several years. One hearing scheduled for July 14, 2020 was postponed for the 18th time because Parovic’s lawyer could not locate him and he did not appear in court. The Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor separated and dismissed the case against Parovic on February 8, 2021 due to his mental health issues. The trial of the former policemen was most recently postponed in July 2022 when one of the defendant’s lawyers asked for the prosecutor and presiding judge to be removed from the case. The outcome remains pending.

charges: terrorism, attempting to stage a coup and violently overthrow the government
chargesCategories: coup activity
trialRelevantInfo: In 2017, the special prosecutor arrested 14 people for attempting to violently overthrow the government with the intent of proclaiming electoral victory for their party and preventing the country from joining the NATO alliance. Those arrested included opposition coalition Democratic Front (DF) leaders Andrija Mandic and Milan Knezevic, who were stripped of their parliamentary immunity and indicted for the crime. Ananije Nikic was initially indicted alongside the defendants in this case, but his case was separated before it was sent to trial, so he will not be included in this trial description. Shishmakov and Popov were Russian military intelligence staffers and were tried in absentia, Dikic was the former commander of an elite Serbian police unit, Ristic and Bogicevic were Serbian citizens and were tried in absentia. The Russians were suspected of being part of an operation by the Russian military intelligence agency formerly known as G.R.U.. On May 9, 2019, the Podgorica High Court convicted Mandic, Knezevic, Shishmakov, Popov, Dikic, Ristic, Bogicevic, and 6 others on terrorism charges for plotting a failed coup. Shishmakov and Popov were sentenced to 15 and 12 years respectively, Mandic and Knezevic were given 5 years, Dikic was given 8 years, Ristic and Bogicevic received 8 and 7 years respectively, and 6 others received smaller jail terms. The decision was appealed, and on February 5, 2021, Montenegro’s Appeals Court overturned the first-instance verdict due to significant violations of criminal procedure, and sent the case back to the High Court for retrial. The retrial verdict is pending.

name: Sami Ljuta
chargesCategories: atrocity or core crime; murder or killing, incl attempted
trialRelevantInfo: In a case known as the “Monster” case, seven ethnic Albanians were tried for the murder of four boys and an adult man in 2012 in North Macedonia. In June 2014, the Skopje Criminal Court convicted the defendants and sentenced all six to life in prison. The conviction sparked protests by ethnic Albanians. The verdict was appealed, and the Court of Appeals upheld the first instance judgment. On November 24, 2017, the Supreme Court quashed the first instance verdict and sent the case back for retrial. On February 23, 2021, the Skopje Criminal Court acquitted Sami Ljuta but convicted the other five defendants. Alil Demir, Affirm Ismailovic, Sami Ljuta, and Agim Ismailovic were sentenced to life in prison for terrorism, Haki Aziri was sentenced to 9 years for aiding an act of terrorism, and Fezji Aziri was sentenced to 15 years in prison for aiding and committing terrorism. Ali Demiri and Afrim Ismailovic were convicted in absentia.

trialRelevantInfo: The trial of 33 men, including five opposition leaders and a former interior minister Mitko Cavkov, for violently attacking the capital began in August 2018. On April 27, 2017, a bloody riot broke out after masked nationalist demonstrators stormed the Skopje assembly to protest the vote for a new parliamentary speaker. The defendants were charged with terrorist endangerment of the constitutional order. In December 2018, North Macedonian parliament passed a much-disputed Amnesty Law that absolved 15 of the initially 33 indicted participants of all charges. 5 of the pardoned defendants were former VMRO DPMNE MPs whose votes were needed to pass a historic agreement with Greece. On March 15, 2019, the Skopje Criminal Court acquitted Igor Durlovski and convicted 16 of the defendants, handing down sentences between 7 and 15 years. Covkov received 18 years; Peshov, Lazarov, Gjoshevski, Epic, Cento, Trajkovski, and Mitrevski received 15 years; Mihajlovski received 14 years; Popovski received 13 years; Dodevski and Jug received 12 years; Radulov received 10 years; Vaselevski received 8 years; and Alimi received 7 years.

name: Pavlo Lazarenko
position_desc: former Prime Minister of Ukraine and Member of Parliament
position_desc_fr: ancien Premier ministre de l'Ukraine et membre du Parlement
accusedNotes: After resigning from the post of Prime Minister in 1997, Lazarenko continued his political career as MP. In 1998, Swiss authorities opened a case against Lazarenko for alleged money laundering. In 1999, before Ukrainian authorities opened a case on state funds expropriation against him, Lazarenko fled to the USA, where he also faced money laundering charges. In 2006, he was sentenced to 97 months of imprisonment in the USA, where he resides till the present. In 2004, he was ranked among the top 10 corrupt officials in the world by Transparency International. In 2000, the Prosecutor General of Ukraine officially opened criminal cases against Lazarenko for the alleged organization of Shcherban and Momot murders in the interest of Yulia Tymoshenko. In 2002, the criminal proceedings regarding the Hetman murder followed. The cases were reopened in 2011 and merged into one case. All charges against Lazarenko in Ukraine are still pending.
charges: Organisation of murders of Vadym Hetman on 22 April 1998 in Kyiv; Yevhen Scherban on 3 November 1996 in Donetsk; Oleksandr Momot on 16 May 1996 in Donetsk

accusedNotes: Kulev, the collaborator of the 'Kushnir gang', was the direct executor of Hetman's murder. Kulev was discovered by chance when he started a debauch in one of Luhansk's nightclubs. Having been detained for hooliganism and unlawful possession of weapons, he has declared involvement in other crimes, among which was the murder of Hetman. Kulev was sentenced to life by the Appellate Court of Luhansk Region in 2003. In 2004 Kulev said that he had slandered himself and his accomplices, and also called Lazarenko the person who ordered the murder under pressure from the senior investigator for particularly important cases of the GPU Valery Silina and under the threat of reprisals against him and his family. He was sentenced for life by the Appellate Court of Luhansk Region in 2003. His appeal to the Supreme Court of Ukraine regarding absence of selfish motive in Momot's murder and absence of intent to kill multiple persons in Shcherban's murder was dismissed. He served the sentence in the Slovyanoserbsk colony of Luhansk region, from which he fled in 2014 after the assault of LDPR militant. The State Penitentiary Service of Ukraine has no information about his recent whereabouts.

trialRelevantInfo: Veselin “Batko” Vlahovic, a Montenegrin Serb former paramilitary commander serving with the Bosnian Serb paramilitary units, was accused of war crimes including murder, rape, and robbery against Bosniaks and Croats in Sarajevo in 1992. Vlahovic was extradited from Spain on August 26, 2010 to face trial in the Bosnia war crimes court for over 60 charges, including the rape, murder, and torture of civilians in Sarajevo. On March 29, 2013, the court convicted Vlahovic of 60 charges, acquitted him of 6 charges, and sentenced him to the maximum prison sentence of 45 years. Vlahovic appealed his sentence, and on June 18, 2014, the appeals chamber of the Bosnian state court acquitted Vlahovic of one of the 60 counts in his indictment and shortened his sentence to 42 years. Vlahovic has been previously sentenced to 12 years in prison in Montenegro, though he escaped jail, and is wanted for armed robbery in Spain and murder in Serbia.
